main.summary: The Universal Gate chapter explains that Guanyin is so called because the bodhisattva hears the cries of beings in suffering and rescues them, giving fearlessness in every kind of danger. It also tells how Guanyin appears in whatever form each being needs in order to teach, and closes with verses that restate the benefit of calling the name.
main.translation:
At that time the bodhisattva Akshayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms towards the Buddha, and said: "World-Honoured One, for what reason is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara called Avalokiteshvara?" The Buddha told the bodhisattva Akshayamati: "Good man, if countless hundreds of thousands of millions of living beings are suffering hardship and distress, and hear of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara and call his name with one mind, Avalokiteshvara at once looks upon their cries, and they are all set free. If anyone holds the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara and falls into a great fire, the fire will not burn him, through the majestic spiritual power of this bodhisattva. If he is swept away by a great flood and calls the name, he will at once find a shallow place. If hundreds of thousands of millions of living beings, seeking gold, silver, lapis lazuli, giant clam shell, agate, coral, amber, pearls and other treasures, go out upon the great sea, and a black wind blows their ship and drives it to the land of the rakshasa demons, and even a single one among them calls the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, all of them will be freed from the danger of the rakshasas. For this reason he is called Avalokiteshvara. And if someone is about to be killed and calls the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, the knives and staves in the attackers' hands will break into pieces, and he will be set free. If the whole world of three thousand great thousands were filled with yakshas and rakshasas who wished to come and torment people, and they heard someone call the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, these evil demons could not even look at him with an evil eye, let alone harm him. If a person, guilty or not guilty, is bound in shackles, cangues and chains, and calls the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, all of them will be broken, and he will be set free. If the whole world of three thousand great thousands were filled with hostile bandits, and a leader of merchants were leading a company of traders carrying heavy treasure along a dangerous road, and one among them were to cry out: 'Good men, do not be afraid. All of you should call with one mind the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara. This bodhisattva can give fearlessness to living beings; if you call his name, you will be freed from these hostile bandits.' Then the merchants, hearing this, would all cry out together: 'Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara!' Because they called his name, they would be set free.

"Akshayamati, the majestic spiritual power of the bodhisattva-mahasattva Avalokiteshvara is as towering as this. If living beings have much desire, and constantly think of and revere Avalokiteshvara, they will be freed from desire. If they have much anger, and constantly think of and revere Avalokiteshvara, they will be freed from anger. If they have much ignorance, and constantly think of and revere Avalokiteshvara, they will be freed from ignorance.

"Akshayamati, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara has such great majestic spiritual power and brings so much benefit; therefore living beings should always hold him in mind. If a woman wishes for a son, and bows to and makes offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, she will bear a son of merit and wisdom; if she wishes for a daughter, she will bear a daughter of upright and fine appearance. Having planted roots of virtue in the past, they will be loved and respected by all.

"Akshayamati, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara has such power. If living beings revere and bow to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, their merit is not wasted. Therefore all living beings should hold and keep the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara.

"Akshayamati, suppose someone holds the names of sixty-two million bodhisattvas, as many as the sands of the Ganges, and for the whole of his life makes offerings to them of food and drink, clothing, bedding and medicine. What do you think? Would the merit of that good man or good woman be great?" Akshayamati said: "Very great, World-Honoured One." The Buddha said: "Suppose another person holds the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, and even for a single moment bows to him and makes an offering. The merit of those two persons is exactly equal and no different, and it cannot be exhausted in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. Akshayamati, those who hold the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara gain such limitless, boundless benefit of merit."

The bodhisattva Akshayamati said to the Buddha: "World-Honoured One, how does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara travel in this Saha world? How does he teach the Dharma to living beings? What is the power of his skilful means?" The Buddha told the bodhisattva Akshayamati: "Good man, in any land, for living beings who can be saved by the body of a buddha, Avalokiteshvara appears in the body of a buddha and teaches the Dharma. For those who can be saved by the body of a pratyekabuddha, he appears in the body of a pratyekabuddha and teaches the Dharma. For those who can be saved by the body of a hearer (shravaka), he appears in the body of a hearer and teaches the Dharma. For those who can be saved by the body of Brahma, he appears in the body of Brahma. For those who can be saved by the body of Indra, he appears in the body of Indra. For those who can be saved by the body of Ishvara, the god of freedom, he appears in the body of Ishvara. For those who can be saved by the body of Maheshvara, the great god of freedom, he appears in the body of Maheshvara. For those who can be saved by the body of a great general of the heavens, he appears in the body of a great general of the heavens. For those who can be saved by the body of Vaishravana, he appears in the body of Vaishravana. For those who can be saved by the body of a minor king, he appears in the body of a minor king. For those who can be saved by the body of an elder, he appears in the body of an elder. For those who can be saved by the body of a householder, he appears in the body of a householder. For those who can be saved by the body of a government official, he appears in the body of a government official. For those who can be saved by the body of a brahmin, he appears in the body of a brahmin. For those who can be saved by the body of a monk, a nun, a lay man or a lay woman, he appears in the body of a monk, a nun, a lay man or a lay woman, and teaches the Dharma. For those who can be saved by the body of the wife of an elder, householder, official or brahmin, he appears in the body of a woman and teaches the Dharma. For those who can be saved by the body of a boy or a girl, he appears in the body of a boy or a girl and teaches the Dharma. For those who can be saved by the bodies of devas, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, he appears in all of these and teaches the Dharma. For those who can be saved by the body of the vajra-holder, he appears in the body of the vajra-holder and teaches the Dharma.

"Akshayamati, this Avalokiteshvara has perfected such virtues, and in many forms travels through the lands to set living beings free. Therefore you should all make offerings to Avalokiteshvara with one mind. This bodhisattva-mahasattva Avalokiteshvara can give fearlessness in the midst of terror and sudden danger; therefore in this Saha world they all call him the Giver of Fearlessness."

The bodhisattva Akshayamati said to the Buddha: "World-Honoured One, I shall now make an offering to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara." He then took off the necklace of many jewels and pearls from his neck, worth a hundred thousand taels of gold, and gave it to him, saying: "Sir, please accept this gift of the Dharma, this necklace of precious jewels." But the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara would not accept it. Akshayamati said again to Avalokiteshvara: "Sir, out of pity for us, please accept this necklace." Then the Buddha told Avalokiteshvara: "Out of pity for this bodhisattva Akshayamati and the fourfold assembly, and for the devas, nagas, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, accept this necklace." Then Avalokiteshvara, out of pity for the fourfold assembly and for the devas, nagas, humans and non-humans, accepted the necklace, divided it into two parts, and offered one part to Shakyamuni Buddha and one part to the stupa of the Buddha Prabhutaratna. "Akshayamati, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara has such sovereign spiritual power, and travels in the Saha world."

At that time the bodhisattva Akshayamati asked in verse:

World-Honoured One, complete in wonderful marks,
I ask once more about him:
For what reason is this child of the Buddha
Called Avalokiteshvara?

The Honoured One, complete in wonderful marks,
Answered Akshayamati in verse.
Listen to the practice of Avalokiteshvara,
Who answers well in every place.
His great vow is as deep as the sea;
Through ages beyond thought,
He has served many hundreds of millions of buddhas
And made great, pure vows.
I shall tell you in brief:
To hear his name and to see his body,
To keep him in mind, is not to pass in vain;
It can put an end to all the sufferings of existence.
Suppose someone with harmful intent
Pushed you into a great pit of fire:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And the pit of fire turns into a pool.
Or if you drift on the great sea,
In danger from dragons, fish and demons:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And the waves cannot drown you.
Or if you are on the peak of Mount Sumeru,
And someone pushes you off:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And you will stand in the sky like the sun.
Or if evil men chase you,
And you fall from the Vajra Mountain:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And not a hair will be harmed.
Or if you are surrounded by hostile bandits,
Each holding a knife to harm you:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And they will all at once feel kindness.
Or if you suffer the king's punishment,
About to be executed and your life to end:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And the blades will break into pieces.
Or if you are imprisoned in cangue and chains,
Your hands and feet bound in shackles:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And you will be released and set free.
Curses and poisonous drugs
Meant to harm your body:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And they will fall back on the one who sent them.
Or if you meet evil rakshasas,
Poisonous dragons and demons:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And none will dare to harm you then.
If fierce beasts surround you,
Their sharp fangs and claws terrible:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And they will flee to the boundless distance.
Vipers, snakes and scorpions,
Their poisonous breath burning like smoke and fire:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And at the sound of your call they turn away.
Clouds and thunder, rolling drums and flashing lightning,
Hail falling and great rain pouring:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And in that moment they scatter.
Living beings in distress,
With countless sufferings pressing on their bodies:
Avalokiteshvara's wondrous wisdom and power
Can save the world from suffering.
Complete in the power of spiritual penetrations,
Practising widely the skilful means of wisdom,
In the lands of the ten directions,
There is no place where he does not appear.
All the many evil paths of rebirth,
Hells, hungry ghosts and animals,
And the sufferings of birth, age, sickness and death,
He gradually brings them all to an end.
The true contemplation, the pure contemplation,
The vast contemplation of wisdom,
The contemplation of compassion and of kindness:
Always to be wished for, always to be gazed upon.
Light without stain, pure light,
The sun of wisdom that breaks all darkness,
Able to subdue the calamities of wind and fire,
And shine on the world everywhere.
A body of compassion, with precepts like thunder,
A mind of kindness like a wondrous great cloud,
Pouring the rain of the Dharma, sweet as dew,
He puts out the flames of affliction.
In lawsuits that go before officials,
In terror in the midst of battle lines:
Think of the power of Avalokiteshvara,
And all your enemies will retreat and scatter.
The wondrous sound, the sound of Avalokiteshvara,
The Brahma sound, the sound of the rising tide,
Surpass the sounds of the world;
Therefore always keep him in mind,
Thought after thought, and do not doubt.
Avalokiteshvara, pure and holy,
In suffering, distress, death and calamity
Is able to be a refuge and support.
Complete in every virtue,
He looks on living beings with eyes of kindness;
His store of blessings is a limitless sea:
Therefore you should bow your head to him.

At that time the bodhisattva Dharanimdhara rose from his seat, came forward and said to the Buddha: "World-Honoured One, if any living beings hear this chapter on the sovereign works of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara and the spiritual power of his universal gate, you should know that the merit of such persons is not small." When the Buddha spoke this Universal Gate chapter, eighty-four thousand living beings in the assembly all gave rise to the mind of unequalled, unsurpassed complete awakening.

keyLines.line: 觀世音菩薩，以何因緣名觀世音
keyLines.en: for what reason is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara called Avalokiteshvara?
keyLines.note: Where the chapter begins: the Bodhisattva Akshayamati asks where Guanyin's name comes from. The Buddha's answer is that when beings in suffering call the name with one mind, the bodhisattva perceives their voices and frees them.

keyLines.line: 若有持是觀世音菩薩名者，設入大火，火不能燒
keyLines.en: If someone holds the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara and falls into a great fire, the fire will not burn him.
keyLines.note: The first of a list of benefits from calling the name: fire, flood, the rakshasa demons, knives and staves, fetters, and bandits. These are popularly called the 'seven dangers'.

keyLines.line: 是菩薩能以無畏施於眾生
keyLines.en: This bodhisattva is able to give fearlessness to living beings.
keyLines.note: Words of the merchant leader to his companions, naming Guanyin's central virtue: giving fearlessness. For this reason beings in this world call him the Giver of Fearlessness.

keyLines.line: 若多愚癡，常念恭敬觀世音菩薩，便得離癡
keyLines.en: If they have much ignorance, and constantly think of and revere Avalokiteshvara, they will be freed from ignorance.
keyLines.note: The chapter goes on to say that calling the name also works against lust (desire), anger and ignorance, the three poisons. It moves from rescue from outer dangers to inner change.

keyLines.line: 應以佛身得度者，觀世音菩薩即現佛身而為說法
keyLines.en: For those who can be saved by the body of a buddha, Avalokiteshvara appears in the body of a buddha and teaches the Dharma.
keyLines.note: The start of Guanyin's 'universal gate' manifestations: whatever form a being can be taught through, Guanyin appears in that form. The list runs from a buddha to boys and girls and the eight kinds of beings of the sutras, adding up to the thirty-three forms.

keyLines.line: 世尊妙相具，我今重問彼，佛子何因緣，名為觀世音
keyLines.en: World-Honoured One, complete in wonderful marks, I ask once more about him: for what reason is this child of the Buddha called Avalokiteshvara?
keyLines.note: The opening of the verse section: Akshayamati asks again, in verse, about the origin of the name. The Buddha answers in verse and restates the dangers and rescues of the prose part.

keyLines.line: 宏誓深如海，歷劫不思議，侍多千億佛，發大清淨願
keyLines.en: His great vow is as deep as the sea; through ages beyond thought he has served many hundreds of millions of buddhas and made great, pure vows.
keyLines.note: The verses say what lies at the root of Guanyin: a great vow as deep as the sea, ages of serving hundreds of millions of buddhas, and great pure vows.

keyLines.line: 妙音觀世音、梵音海潮音，勝彼世間音，是故須常念，念念勿生疑
keyLines.en: The wonderful sound, the sound of Avalokiteshvara, the Brahma sound, the sound of the rising tide, surpass the sounds of the world; therefore always keep him in mind, thought after thought, and do not doubt.
keyLines.note: A closing verse: the sound of Guanyin is compared to a wonderful sound, a Brahma sound and the sound of the sea tide, and said to surpass any sound in the world. It urges people to keep him in mind at all times, without doubt.

glossary.note: A translation of the Sanskrit Avalokiteshvara (also rendered 'Guanzizai'): 'guan' is to contemplate, and 'shiyin' is the cries of the beings of the world. During the Tang dynasty (618-907) the name was shortened to 'Guanyin' to avoid the personal name of Emperor Taizong, Li Shimin.
The bodhisattva who asks the Buddha in this chapter. His name means 'of inexhaustible mind', whose wisdom and compassion never run out.

glossary.en: shi wuwei zhe - the Giver of Fearlessness
glossary.note: Guanyin is so called because he can free beings from fear in times of terror and sudden danger.
'Pu' means universal, and 'men' is a gate of skilful means into the Dharma. The meaning is that Guanyin takes every way open to him, appearing in whatever form suits the occasion in order to teach.
Sanskrit rakshasa, a demon that eats people. The 'land of the rakshasas' in this chapter means a dangerous place out at sea.

glossary.en: ying yi ... shen de du - those who can be saved by the body of ...
glossary.note: 'For those who can be saved by such-and-such a body, he appears in that body' is the pattern of the universal-gate manifestations: whatever kind of person a being can best be taught by, Guanyin takes that form.

glossary.en: sizhong, tian long babu - the fourfold assembly and the eight kinds of beings
glossary.note: The fourfold assembly is monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen. Devas, nagas, yakshas and the rest are the eight kinds of beings often found in the sutras as protectors of the Dharma.

glossary.en: fu bu tang juan - merit is not wasted
glossary.note: 'Tang juan' means to throw away for nothing. The line says that the merit planted by revering and bowing to Guanyin does not come to nothing.

main.background: This is the 25th chapter, in volume seven, of the Lotus Sutra (Saddharma Pundarika), translated by Kumarajiva; circulated on its own it is called the Guanyin Sutra. The prose part is Kumarajiva's translation. By tradition the verses were not in his translation, and the verses in the usual text are taken from the supplementary translation in the Tianpin Miaofa Lianhua Jing of the Sui dynasty (581-618). East Asian devotion to Guanyin rests mainly on this chapter, and the thirty-three manifestations later gave rise to many different images of Guanyin.
